title: Bases and subspaces
objectives: Build a topology from a basis and give a subset the subspace topology.

screens.title: Building from pieces
screens.prose: On $X = \{a, b, c, d\}$ take the pieces $\{a\}$, $\{a, b\}$, $\{c\}$ and $\{c, d\}$, shaded below. The grid lists all 16 subsets. Unions of pieces include the empty union, $\varnothing$.
screens.question: Tap every subset that is a union of pieces.

hints.text: A union holds $b$ only if it holds $\{a, b\}$, so it also holds $a$.
$\{b\}$ alone is no union of pieces.
Choose from $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{a, b\}\}$ and $\{\varnothing, \{c\}, \{c, d\}\}$: $3 \times 3 = 9$ unions.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Build each union from a choice in $\{a, b\}$ and a choice in $\{c, d\}$.

byKey.r1c3: $\{b\}$ is no union of pieces: the only piece holding $b$ also holds $a$.
byKey.r1c1: You missed $\varnothing$, the union of no pieces.
byKey.r2c1: $\{d\}$ is no union: the only piece holding $d$ also holds $c$.

explain.text: From the $a, b$ side choose $\varnothing$, $\{a\}$ or $\{a, b\}$; from the $c, d$ side likewise. That gives $3 \times 3 = 9$ unions, and they form a topology.

screens.title: When pieces are a basis
screens.prose: A family $\mathcal{B}$ is a **basis** when its pieces cover $X$. Also, each point of an overlap $B_1 \cap B_2$ lies in a piece inside it. The topology it **generates** is every union of pieces.

state.caption: Pieces $\{a, b\}$ and $\{b, c\}$ on $\{a, b, c\}$; dashed: their overlap.

screens.question: Is $\{\{a, b\}, \{b, c\}\}$ a basis of $\{a, b, c\}$?

options.text: No: the overlap $\{b\}$ contains no piece holding $b$.
Yes: the two pieces cover $\{a, b, c\}$.
options.why: Covering is only the first condition. The overlap condition fails at $b$.

options.text: No: their union is not a piece.
options.why: Unions of pieces need not be pieces; they are the open sets the basis makes.

feedback.correct: Right. The overlap test fails at $b$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test the second condition at the point $b$.

explain.text: The only pieces holding $b$ are $\{a, b\}$ and $\{b, c\}$, and neither lies in $\{b\}$. So the unions of pieces would miss $\{b\}$, breaking the intersection axiom.

screens.title: Generated as a subbasis
screens.prose: We can still use $\{a, b\}$ and $\{b, c\}$ as a **subbasis**: first add all finite intersections, then take all unions.
screens.question: Which sets are in the topology it generates? Select all that apply.

options.why: No intersection or union isolates $a$: every set built holds $b$ with $a$.

hints.text: Unions of $\{b\}$, $\{a, b\}$, $\{b, c\}$ add $X$; add $\varnothing$ too.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the intersection $\{b\}$, then take unions.

explain.text: The intersections add $\{b\}$, and unions add $\{a, b, c\}$. The topology is $\{\varnothing, \{b\}, \{a, b\}, \{b, c\}, X\}$.

screens.title: Bases you already know
screens.prose: In a metric space every open set is a union of open balls: each point has a ball inside it. On $\mathbb{R}$ we can even shrink the family.
screens.question: Which family is a countable basis of $\mathbb{R}$?

options.text: All open intervals $(p, q)$ with rational $p < q$
All open intervals $(p, q)$ with real $p < q$
options.why: That is a basis, but not countable: there is one interval per real pair.
They miss every whole number, and no union of them gives $(0.3, 0.6)$.

hints.text: Between any two reals lies a rational.
Round $x$ inside $U$ sits an interval with rational ends.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The family must be a basis and countable.

explain.text: If $x \in U$ open, some $(x - r, x + r) \subseteq U$, and rationals $p \in (x - r, x)$, $q \in (x, x + r)$ give $x \in (p, q) \subseteq U$. There are countably many rational pairs.

screens.title: Open in a subset
screens.prose: For $Y \subseteq X$ the **subspace topology** is $\tau_Y = \{U \cap Y : U \in \tau\}$. Take $Y = \{0\} \cup \{1, \tfrac12, \tfrac13, \dots\}$ inside $\mathbb{R}$.
screens.question: Which singletons are open in $Y$?

options.text: None: singletons are never open in $\mathbb{R}$
options.why: Open in $Y$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}$. $(0.4, 0.6) \cap Y = \{\tfrac12\}$.
Every interval round 0 holds some $\tfrac1n$, so no $U \cap Y$ equals $\{0\}$.

hints.text: Round 0 every interval catches infinitely many points of $Y$.

feedback.correct: Right. Each $\tfrac1n$ is isolated in $Y$; 0 is not.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test each point with a small open interval.

explain.text: A small interval round $\tfrac1n$ meets $Y$ only in $\{\tfrac1n\}$, so that singleton is open in $Y$. Every interval round 0 holds points $\tfrac1n$, so $\{0\}$ is not. Likewise $\mathbb{Z}$ inside $\mathbb{R}$ is discrete.

screens.title: A subspace of a finite space
screens.prose: Take $\tau = \{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{a, b\}, X\}$ on $X = \{a, b, c\}$ and the subset $Y = \{b, c\}$.
screens.question: Which sets are in $\tau_Y$? Select all that apply.

options.why: No open set of $X$ meets $Y$ in exactly $\{c\}$: every one holding $c$ is $X$.

hints.text: Intersect each of the four open sets with $\{b, c\}$.

feedback.correct: Right. A Sierpiński space on $\{b, c\}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compute $U \cap Y$ for each open $U$.

explain.text: The intersections are $\varnothing$, $\varnothing$, $\{b\}$ and $\{b, c\}$. So $\tau_Y = \{\varnothing, \{b\}, \{b, c\}\}$, the Sierpiński space with $b$ the open point.

screens.title: An open subspace
screens.prose: Let $Y$ be open in $X$. We prove: $W \subseteq Y$ is open in $Y$ exactly when $W$ is open in $X$. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: If $W$ is open in $Y$, then $W = U \cap Y$ for some $U$ open in $X$, by definition of $\tau_Y$.
$U$ and $Y$ are both open in $X$, so $W = U \cap Y$ is open in $X$, by the intersection axiom.
Conversely, if $W \subseteq Y$ is open in $X$, then $W = W \cap Y$ with $W \in \tau$.
Every set open in $Y$ is open in $X$, whatever $Y$ is.
lines.why: Not without $Y$ open: $[0, 0.5)$ is open in $[0, 1]$ but not in $\mathbb{R}$.

hints.text: Where does the proof use that $Y$ is open?

feedback.correct: Right. Openness of $Y$ is used once, in the intersection.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Write $W = U \cap Y$ first.

byKey.d1: You dropped the hypothesis that $Y$ is open. Without it the claim fails.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: $W = U \cap Y$ is an intersection of two open sets of $X$, so it is open in $X$. Conversely, an open $W \subseteq Y$ is its own intersection with $Y$. The hypothesis that $Y$ is open is essential.

options.text: Open in $Y$, as $U \cap Y$; not open in $\mathbb{R}$
Open in neither, since it contains its end 0
options.why: You judged openness in $\mathbb{R}$. In $Y$ there is nothing below 0, so $W$ is a relative ball round 0.

options.text: Open in both, since it is open in $Y$
options.why: Every interval of $\mathbb{R}$ round 0 holds negatives, outside $W$.

hints.text: Open in $Y$ means some open $U$ of $\mathbb{R}$ gives $W = U \cap Y$.

feedback.correct: Right. Openness depends on the space.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test openness in $Y$ and in $\mathbb{R}$ separately.

byKey.neither: You read "open in $Y$" as "open in $\mathbb{R}$". In $Y$, $W = (-0.5, 0.5) \cap Y$ is open.
byKey.both: You carried openness from $Y$ up to $\mathbb{R}$. That needs $Y$ open, and $[0, 1]$ is not.

explain.text: $W = (-0.5, 0.5) \cap [0, 1]$ is open in $Y$ by definition. In $\mathbb{R}$, every interval round 0 holds negatives, so $W$ is not open there. Open in $Y$ equals open in $X$ only when $Y$ is open.

screens.title: The whole subspace
screens.prose: The axioms put $Y$ in $\tau_Y$, since $Y = X \cap Y$. Take $Y = [0, 1]$, which is closed in $\mathbb{R}$.
screens.question: Is $[0, 1]$ open in the subspace $[0, 1]$?

options.text: Yes: $[0, 1] = \mathbb{R} \cap [0, 1]$, so it is open in $Y$, though closed in $\mathbb{R}$.
No: it is closed, so it cannot be open.
options.why: Open and closed are not opposites. $Y$ is always both open and closed in itself.

options.text: No: the ends 0 and 1 have no room.
options.why: Room is measured in $Y$. The relative ball $[0, 0.1)$ round 0 lies inside $Y$.

feedback.correct: Right. Every space is open in itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Apply the definition with $U = \mathbb{R}$.

explain.text: $\mathbb{R}$ is open, and $\mathbb{R} \cap Y = Y$, so $Y$ is open in $Y$. Being closed in $\mathbb{R}$ does not change that.

screens.title: Bases and subspaces by machine
screens.prose: Write `generate(B)`, every union of pieces with $\varnothing$ included, and `is_basis(X, B)`. Then `subspace(tau, Y)` returns $\{U \cap Y\}$. The hidden helpers `T(...)` and `norm(...)` build and print families. Checking cases is evidence, not proof.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests, compared exactly through norm. They cover the four-point basis (9 sets), the singleton basis and two non-bases. One family becomes a basis once $\{b\}$ is added. Two test subspaces. The first Check starts Python in the browser, about 4 s once.

hints.text: For `is_basis`, test every point of every overlap.

feedback.correct: Right. All three agree with the screens.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Remember $\varnothing$, the cover test and the overlap test.

explain.text: The four pieces generate the nine sets of the hook. $\{\{a, b\}, \{b, c\}\}$ fails the overlap test until $\{b\}$ joins it. The subspace on $\{b, c\}$ is the Sierpiński space.

screens.title: Interior of a portfolio triangle
screens.prose: Long-only weights on three assets form the triangle $\{w \ge 0, w_1 + w_2 + w_3 = 1\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Every 3D ball leaves its plane, so it has no interior in $\mathbb{R}^3$. In the subspace topology, strictly positive weights form an open set. Grow the relative ball round the equal-weight portfolio.
screens.question: What is the largest radius of a relative ball round $(\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$ inside the triangle? Give four decimal places.

widget.accept: 0.4082: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6}$, the distance to the edge midpoint $(0.5, 0.5, 0)$.

hints.text: The nearest boundary points are the edge midpoints.

feedback.correct: Right. The inradius of a triangle of side $\sqrt2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the distance from the centre to an edge midpoint.

byKey.vertex: $\sqrt{\tfrac23}$ is the distance to a corner. The edges are nearer.
byKey.third: $\tfrac13$ is the smallest weight, not a distance in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

explain.text: The distance to $(0.5, 0.5, 0)$ is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt6} \approx 0.4082$, the inradius of a triangle of side $\sqrt2$. An optimiser's "interior solution" means interior in the triangle, not in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

ideas: A basis covers $X$, and each point of an overlap has a piece inside the overlap. Its topology is every union of pieces. A subbasis first adds finite intersections.
Open balls form a basis of a metric topology, and intervals with rational ends a countable basis of $\mathbb{R}$.
The subspace topology is $\tau_Y = \{U \cap Y\}$: $[0, 0.5)$ is open in $[0, 1]$ but not in $\mathbb{R}$. When $Y$ is open, open in $Y$ means open in $X$ and inside $Y$.

formula.name: Subspace topology
formula.note: $Y$ is always open in itself, even when closed in $X$.

summary.trap: Open in $Y$ is not open in $X$: $[0, 0.5)$ is open in $[0, 1]$ yet not open in $\mathbb{R}$.

options.why: You looked for intervals inside $\mathbb{Z}$. Relative openness only needs $U \cap \mathbb{Z}$.
That is the cofinite topology. Here each singleton is open.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Intersect a short interval with $\mathbb{Z}$.

explain.text: $(n - \tfrac12, n + \tfrac12)$ meets $\mathbb{Z}$ only in $\{n\}$. Every singleton is open, so every subset is.

quiz.prose: On $\{a, b, c\}$ take the basis $\{\{a\}, \{a, b\}, \{a, c\}\}$.
quiz.question: How many open sets does it generate, $\varnothing$ included?

feedback.generic: Not quite. List every union of pieces.

byKey.pieces: You counted only the pieces. Unions add $X$, and $\varnothing$ counts too.
byKey.noempty: You left out $\varnothing$, the union of no pieces.

explain.text: The unions are $\varnothing$, $\{a\}$, $\{a, b\}$, $\{a, c\}$ and $\{a, b\} \cup \{a, c\} = X$. That is 5 open sets.

quiz.question: Is $W = (1, 2)$ open in $Y$, and is it open in $\mathbb{R}$?

options.why: $(1, 2)$ is an open interval of $\mathbb{R}$. Since $Y$ is open, the two notions agree here.

options.text: Open in neither, since 2 is the end of $Y$
options.why: 2 is not in $W$, so it needs no room.

feedback.correct: Right. For open $Y$ the notions match.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the open-subspace result.

explain.text: $(1, 2)$ is open in $\mathbb{R}$ and lies in $Y$. Because $Y$ is open, open in $Y$ is the same as open in $\mathbb{R}$ inside $Y$.
